title: Rings, unity, and subrings
terms: ring; commutative ring; ring with unity; subring; distributive laws; additive identity; multiplicative identity.

exposition.text:
A ring has an Abelian additive group, an associative multiplication, and both distributive laws.
A commutative ring also has commutative multiplication. A ring with unity has a multiplica-
tive identity 1; when discussing domains and fields, require 1 ̸= 0. The book allows rings with-
out unity and subrings that need not share the ambient identity.
With that convention, a nonempty subset is a subring when closed under subtraction and mul-
tiplication. Some modern texts instead require rings and subrings to preserve 1, so conventions
must be stated. The additive identity always absorbs multiplication: 0r = r0 = 0. Matrix rings
of size at least two are standard noncommutative examples, while nZ is a ring without unity for
n > 1.
The two distributive laws are r(s + t) = rs + rt and (r + s)t = rt + st. For example, r0 =
r(0 + 0) = r0 + r0 gives r0 = 0 by additive cancellation; similarly 0r = 0. The two distributive
laws must both be checked when a proposed multiplication is not commutative.

question.text:
Under the book convention allowing a subring to have a different identity, what is the multi-
plicative identity of S = {0, 3, 6, 9, 12} ⊆ Z ?
15
(A) 0 (B) 3 (C) 6 (D) 9 (E) 12

solution.text:
An identity e ∈ S must satisfy 3e ≡ 3 (mod 15), so e ≡ 1 (mod 5). The unique such
element of S is 6. Every member is a multiple of 3, and multiplication by 6 fixes all of
them modulo 15.

question.text:
Which subset of M (R) is a subring under ordinary operations?
2
(A) All matrices of trace zero
(B) All matrices of determinant one
(C) All symmetric matrices
(D) All upper triangular matrices
(E) All invertible matrices

solution.text:
Upper triangular matrices are closed under subtraction and multiplication and contain zero.
The trace-zero and symmetric conditions fail under multiplication; determinant-one and
invertible matrices do not contain the additive zero.

question.text:
On the additive group Z , define a new multiplication by a ∗ b = 0 for all a, b. With ordinary
6
addition, this structure is which of the following?
(A) Not a ring because multiplication has no cancellation
(B) Not a ring because 1 ∗ 1 ̸= 1
(C) A commutative ring without a multiplicative identity
(D) A field of characteristic six
(E) A noncommutative ring with identity zero

solution.text:
Zero multiplication is associative, commutative, and distributive over addition, so the
ring axioms hold. An identity would have to satisfy e ∗ 1 = 1, but every product is zero.
Cancellation and a unity are not required by the stated ring convention.

question.text:

Let R be a unital ring and e ∈ R satisfy e = e. Set S = {ere : r ∈ R}. Which statement
always holds?
(A) S is a subring whose identity is e.
(B) S is a subring whose identity must equal 1 .
R
(C) S is commutative.
(D) S has no nonzero zero divisors.
(E) S is an additive subgroup but need not be closed under multiplication.

solution.text:
2
Subtraction gives ere − ese = e(r − s)e. A product is (ere)(ese) = e(res)e, using e = e,
so S is a subring. Also e(ere) = (ere)e = ere. The ambient identity need not belong to S;
a matrix projection provides a proper corner subring.

question.text:
On Z, retain ordinary addition and define a ∗ b = a. Which of the following laws hold?
I. (a ∗ b) ∗ c = a ∗ (b ∗ c).
II. a ∗ (b + c) = a ∗ b + a ∗ c.
III. (a + b) ∗ c = a ∗ c + b ∗ c.
(A) I only (B) II only (C) I and II only (D) I and III only (E) All three

solution.text:
Both sides in I equal a, and both sides in III equal a + b. In II the left side is a, while the
right side is 2a, so this law fails, for instance at a = 1. Associative multiplication and an
Abelian additive group do not suffice for a ring; both distributive laws must hold.
